unit.title: Doubles Strategy
unit.summary: Position on the court, the third-shot drop, moving as a team, middle-ball calls, stacking, switching, poaching and targeting.

lessons.title: Two up, two back
lessons.objective: Explain the standard court positions in doubles.

payload.prompt: Your team is on the near side. Tap where both of you stand in two-up.

diagram.alt: Doubles court from above. Your team is on the near side of the net, and the kitchen line and the baseline are both marked.

explanation.correct: Two-up means both partners are at the kitchen line, side by side, ready to volley. It is the position most teams are trying to reach.
explanation.incorrect: Two-back at the baseline is where a team often starts the point, not where it wants to finish. Two-up is both at the kitchen line.
explanation.sayThisLine: Two-up means both of us are at the kitchen line.

payload.prompt: Why do doubles teams aim for 'two-up'?

options.text: It lets both partners control the net and volley down at the opponents
It's easier to run from the baseline
It gives you more space to hit drives
It's called that because there are two players

explanation.correct: At the kitchen line you can volley balls out of the air and hit down on anything that sits up, so the other team feels the pressure.
explanation.incorrect: The name just means both players are up at the kitchen line. The reason teams want it is net control, not running room or drive space.
explanation.sayThisLine: Two-up: both of us at the kitchen line, in control of the net.

payload.prompt: Match each court position to its description.

pairs.definition: Both partners at the kitchen line, side by side, in control of the net.
Both partners back at the baseline, which is where the serving team starts the point.
The phase when a team is walking up from the baseline toward the kitchen line.

distractorDefinitions: Both players standing in the kitchen
One player sitting out the point

explanation.summary: The serving team starts two-back, moves through transition, and aims to get two-up at the kitchen line.
explanation.sayThisLine: Start two-back, move through transition, get two-up.

payload.prompt: Complete the positioning strategy.
payload.template: In doubles, {{formation}} is the goal because both players can {{control-action}}.

explanation.correct: Two-up is the usual goal: at the kitchen line both partners can volley and take control of the rally.
explanation.incorrect: Two-back is where the point often starts. The aim is two-up, where both partners can volley and attack balls that sit up.
explanation.sayThisLine: Two-up is where we can volley and attack.

payload.prompt: After the serve and return, your team is at the baseline for the third shot. Which is the smart play?

options.text: A soft drop into the kitchen so you have time to advance to the net
A hard drive to end the point immediately
A lob to get them away from the net
Any shot, it doesn't matter

explanation.correct: The third-shot drop is a soft arc into their kitchen. It gives your team time to walk up to the kitchen line, and it is hard for them to attack.
explanation.incorrect: A hard drive can work as a change of pace, but from the baseline it is risky, and a lob can be smashed. The drop is the common, reliable choice.
explanation.sayThisLine: Third shot: soft drop to buy time, then move up.

payload.prompt: Their third shot is coming. Do you rush the net, or move up with care?

situation.narrative: You just returned the serve, and the other team is about to hit their third shot from back near their baseline. It could be a soft drop or a drive.

facts.label: Their shot
facts.value: Not hit yet, could be a drop or a drive

options.label: Move up, but be ready to stop and split step
options.consequence: Smart. A soft drop gives you time to keep moving up, and stopping in balance lets you handle a drive if it comes.
considerations: Most third shots are drops, so you often have time
Balance beats speed
A quick split step covers the drive too

options.label: Sprint to the net without stopping
options.consequence: Risky. If they hit a drive while you are still running, you are caught off balance in mid-court with a ball at your feet.
considerations: You cannot react if you are mid-stride
Mid-court is an awkward place to get hit
It is better to arrive balanced than early

payload.expertNote: Move up when you can, and stop to split step when they hit. Arriving balanced matters more than arriving first.

payload.prompt: From the baseline, your third shot is a hard drive. Is that the usual play?

scene.alt: Third-shot scenario: the serving team hits a hard drive from the baseline while the returners are already up at the kitchen line.

choices.label: No, the drop is the usual play

explanation.correct: A drop is the usual third shot. A drive is a real option, especially when the returners are back, but when they are already at the kitchen line it is harder to do well.
explanation.incorrect: A drive can be smart at the right moment, such as when the returners are still back. It is just not the everyday choice, because it is harder and gives you less time to walk up.
explanation.sayThisLine: A drop is the usual third shot, and a drive is the surprise.

payload.prompt: Complete the third-shot strategy.
payload.template: The {{shot-type}} is the usual third shot because it {{reason}}, while a hard drive from the baseline is {{risk}}.

explanation.correct: The drop gives your team time to walk up to the kitchen line. A hard drive from the baseline gives you less time and is easier for the other team to counter.
explanation.incorrect: The drop is the usual choice because it buys time to move up. A hard drive from the back can work, but it is the riskier shot.
explanation.sayThisLine: The drop buys time. A drive from the back is riskier.

lessons.title: Drop it, then move up
lessons.objective: Understand why the drop buys time to reach the line.

payload.prompt: A soft third-shot drop lands in the kitchen. Your team now has time to advance. True?

scene.alt: Third-shot scenario: soft drop in the kitchen, team has time to move.

choices.label: True, the drop buys us time
False, we still have to hurry

explanation.correct: True. A soft arc takes longer to travel and is hard for them to attack, so your team gets a moment to walk up from the baseline.
explanation.incorrect: A fast ball would leave no time. The soft arc of a drop is exactly what buys your team time to advance.
explanation.sayThisLine: The soft drop buys us time to move up.

payload.prompt: As you advance from the baseline to the kitchen line after a drop, which zone are you crossing?

options.text: The transition zone (no-man's-land), where you're vulnerable if a ball is hit hard
The area behind the baseline
The kitchen
The alley along the sideline

explanation.correct: The transition zone is the mid-court stretch between the baseline and the kitchen line. Balls hit at your feet there are awkward, so a drop buys time to cross it.
explanation.incorrect: After a drop you walk through the middle of the court, between the baseline and the kitchen line. That stretch is the transition zone, often called no-man's-land.
explanation.sayThisLine: The transition zone is the risky middle stretch.

payload.prompt: Complete the third-shot drop strategy.
payload.template: The {{shot-type}} lands in the kitchen and {{what-happens}}, so your team has time to {{action}}.

explanation.correct: The drop takes time, giving your team a window to advance from baseline to the kitchen line.
explanation.incorrect: Drop into kitchen gives time; use that moment to advance.
explanation.sayThisLine: Soft drop buys time to advance to the net.

lessons.title: The transition zone
lessons.objective: Identify no-man's-land and how to cross it.

payload.prompt: Your team is on the near side. Tap the transition zone.

diagram.alt: Doubles court from above, with your team on the near side. The kitchen is beside the net, and the open mid-court sits between the kitchen line and the baseline.

explanation.correct: The transition zone is the mid-court stretch between your baseline and the kitchen line. A fast ball at your feet is awkward there, so a drop buys time to cross it.
explanation.incorrect: The kitchen is right beside the net. The transition zone is the open mid-court behind the kitchen line, where a fast ball can catch you out of position.
explanation.sayThisLine: The transition zone is the risky stretch between the baseline and the kitchen line.

payload.prompt: Put the steps for safely crossing the transition zone in order.

items.text: Hit a soft third-shot drop that lands in the kitchen
items.why: This gives the opponents time to respond and gives you time to advance.

items.text: Start moving forward from the baseline while the ball is in flight
items.why: The drop is already in the air, so you begin your advance immediately.

items.text: Cross the transition zone (mid-court), stopping to split step when they hit
items.why: You move through the risky stretch, but stay balanced when their next shot comes.

items.text: Reach the kitchen line and set yourself in the ready position
items.why: Being set at the line lets you volley whatever comes next.

items.text: You are now two-up at the kitchen line
items.why: Both partners are at the line, which is the position teams are trying to reach.

explanation.correct: Hit the drop, start moving while it is in the air, cross the mid-court with a split step, get set at the line, and you are two-up.
explanation.incorrect: Start with the soft drop, then advance through the transition zone, and finish set at the kitchen line.
explanation.sayThisLine: Drop, move, split step, set at the line.

payload.prompt: Why is the transition zone called 'no-man's-land'?

options.text: Because you're caught in mid-court, neither at the net nor at the baseline, vulnerable to hard shots
Because no one plays in that area
Because the ball isn't allowed there
Because it's too far to run

explanation.correct: You are caught in the middle of the court. Balls hit at your feet there are awkward, and you are not yet at the net where you would have the advantage.
explanation.incorrect: It is not about rules or distance. The zone is risky because you are between the baseline and the net, where low, fast balls are hard to play.
explanation.sayThisLine: No-man's-land is the awkward middle of the court.

payload.prompt: Complete the transition zone concept.
payload.template: The transition zone is {{location}} and is dangerous because {{danger}}; a {{shot-type}} gives you time to cross it.

explanation.correct: The transition zone is mid-court, and it is risky because hard balls at your feet catch you off guard. A soft drop gives your team time to cross it.
explanation.incorrect: The zone is in the middle of the court, not at the net, and you can move fine there. The danger is a hard ball at your feet, which a soft drop helps you avoid.
explanation.sayThisLine: Soft drop buys time to cross the transition zone.

payload.prompt: The ball goes to the left side. Do both partners shift left together?

scene.alt: Doubles scenario: the ball is on the left side of the court, and both partners at the kitchen line slide left.

explanation.correct: Yes. Partners move side by side, like two ends of one rope, so the space between them stays the same and there is no gap to attack.
explanation.incorrect: If only one player moves, a gap opens up between the partners. Shifting together keeps the court covered.
explanation.sayThisLine: Partners move as a unit to cover gaps.

payload.prompt: What is the main reason partners move together as a unit?

options.text: To avoid leaving gaps in coverage and to stay coordinated against the ball movement
Because it looks better
To go faster
Because the rules require it

explanation.correct: Moving together maintains court coverage; gaps are how opponents score.
explanation.incorrect: Coordinated movement keeps coverage tight and prevents opponents from finding openings.
explanation.sayThisLine: Move as a team to cover gaps together.

payload.prompt: A dink pulls your partner wide. Do you slide with them or stay put?

situation.narrative: You and your partner are both at the kitchen line. A dink pulls your partner toward their right sideline, away from you.

facts.label: The risk
facts.value: A gap opening up down the middle

options.label: Slide over with them to keep the middle covered
options.consequence: Good. As your partner moves wide, you shift toward them so the space between you stays small and the middle stays protected.
considerations: Moving together keeps gaps closed
The middle stays covered as you shift
A quick word like 'with you' helps

options.label: Stay where you are while they handle it
options.consequence: A gap opens down the middle. If their shot comes up soft, the other team can attack right through it.
considerations: Standing still stretches the space between you
Moving as a pair keeps the court covered
The middle is left open

payload.expertNote: Doubles partners move like a pair. When one of you is pulled wide, the other shifts too, so the middle stays covered.

lessons.title: Down the middle
lessons.objective: Decide who takes the middle and how to call it.

payload.prompt: A ball comes down the middle between you and your partner. You both go for it without calling. Good?

scene.alt: Doubles scenario: ball comes down the middle between partners.

explanation.correct: Not a good idea. Middle balls are where partners collide or both leave it, so a quick call of 'mine' or 'yours' matters.
explanation.incorrect: Without a call, both players may go for the ball and clash, or both may let it go. A single word avoids both problems.
explanation.sayThisLine: Middle ball: call 'mine' to claim it.

payload.prompt: A dink floats down the middle. Your forehand reaches it, their backhand does. Who takes it?

situation.narrative: The dink is right down the middle between you and your partner. The ball is on your forehand side, and on your partner's backhand side.

options.label: You take it, with a clear call of 'mine'
options.consequence: A good plan. Most players are steadier on the forehand, and a clear call means your partner does not reach for it too.
considerations: Many players trust their forehand more
A quick 'mine' prevents confusion
Your partner can cover the space behind you

options.label: Let your partner take it on the backhand
options.consequence: That works if your partner has a strong backhand and you both agree. Without a call, though, you might both hesitate.
considerations: Some players love the backhand
It needs a clear agreement first
You give up the usual guideline

payload.expertNote: 'Forehand in the middle' is a common guideline, not a rule. It works well for most pairs, but what matters most is that you agree and call it.

statement.speaker: Alex
statement.text: Did you call that ball? We both went for it and I thought you were taking it.

payload.question: What should you say?

options.text: Sorry, that one's on me. Let's say 'mine' or 'yours' on middle balls.
You should have known I wanted it.
It's just a dink, don't worry about it.
I always take middle balls.

payload.translation: Calls like 'mine' and 'yours' prevent collisions and confusion. A missed call is something partners fix together, not something to pin on one person.

followUps.line: Yeah, I should have called it. Next time I'll say 'mine' when I see it coming.
followUps.why: Takes responsibility without making it a big deal.

followUps.line: Let's agree who takes the middle before the next point, so we both know.
followUps.why: Turns the mix-up into a team habit.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You do not need a full strategy lecture. A warm apology and a simple plan for next time is plenty.

payload.prompt: Why do partners call 'mine' or 'yours' on balls in the middle?

options.text: So only one player goes for it, and nobody collides or lets it drop
To distract the other team
Because the rules require a call
To keep track of the score

explanation.correct: A quick call settles who is hitting the ball, so you avoid colliding or both leaving it for the other.
explanation.incorrect: The call is a habit, not a rule. It is not about the score or the other team. It simply keeps two partners from getting in each other's way.
explanation.sayThisLine: I call 'mine' or 'yours' so we don't both go for it.

payload.prompt: Your team is stacked on the right. Tap where you both stand.

diagram.alt: Doubles court from above. Your team is on the near side, and the near side is split into a left half and a right half by the centerline.

explanation.correct: Stacking means both partners line up on the same side of the court, here the right, at the start of the point.
explanation.incorrect: You are stacked on the right, so you are both on the right half. Both on the left would be stacked on the left, and one on each side is the usual split.
explanation.sayThisLine: When we stack, we both start on the same side.

payload.prompt: Put one stacked point in order.

items.text: Both partners line up on the same side before the serve
items.why: That is the stack. The server stands where the score says, and the partner joins on the same side.
Players are free to move once the ball is served, so the stack can come undone.

items.text: Each partner slides to their preferred side
items.why: This is the point of stacking: each player ends up on the side they like.

items.text: The rally goes on with one partner on each side
items.why: From here the point looks like any other doubles point.

explanation.correct: Line up stacked, serve, slide to your preferred sides, and then play the point as usual.
explanation.incorrect: The stack only exists before the serve. Once the ball is served, partners slide to the sides they prefer.
explanation.sayThisLine: We stack at the start, then slide to our sides.

payload.prompt: Complete the sentence about stacking.
payload.template: When a team stacks, both partners line up on the {{start}} side, then slide to their preferred sides once the ball is {{when}}.

explanation.correct: In a stack, both partners start on the same side and then slide to their preferred sides once the ball is in play. Switching sides mid-rally is a separate move.
explanation.incorrect: Partners line up on the same side first, not opposite sides. They move once the ball is served, while it is in play, not after the point is dead.
explanation.sayThisLine: We start on the same side, then slide once it's in play.

payload.prompt: Why would a doubles team use stacking?

options.text: So each partner can play their preferred side, even when the serving order puts them elsewhere
To make the court bigger
Because the rules require it
To avoid ever having to move

explanation.correct: The serving order decides who stands where at the serve. Stacking lets a team line up so that, once the ball is in play, each partner ends up on the side they prefer, such as keeping a forehand in the middle.
explanation.incorrect: Stacking is optional, and it does not change the size of the court or save anyone from moving. It is a way to get each player onto their favorite side.
explanation.sayThisLine: We stack so each of us plays our favorite side.

lessons.title: Poach and target
lessons.objective: Understand poaching and targeting the weaker side.

payload.prompt: A ball heads toward your partner's side. Do you poach it?

situation.narrative: You are both at the net. A ball is heading toward the middle, closer to your partner on the right than to you on the left.

facts.label: Your partner
facts.value: Right side, closer to the ball

facts.label: You
facts.value: Left side, a step farther away

options.label: Poach: step across and volley it yourself
options.consequence: A poach can surprise the other team and win the point, but it only works if you time it and your partner knows. If you miss, you have left a gap.
considerations: Poaching can surprise the other team
It needs timing and a signal to your partner
A missed poach leaves your side open

options.label: Let your partner take it while you cover your side
options.consequence: A solid call. Your partner is closer, so they play it while you stay ready for the reply.
considerations: Your partner is better placed
Staying put keeps your side covered
A quick call confirms who has it

payload.expertNote: Poaching is a bold move, not a default. It works best when it is planned with your partner and the timing feels right.

statement.speaker: Jordan
statement.text: You totally poached my shot and missed. That cost us the point!

payload.question: What should you say?

options.text: Sorry, I should have given you a signal first. Want to agree on one?
I was going for the win, don't be mad.
You should have been ready to back me up.
Poaching is always the right play.

payload.translation: Poaching is aggressive but needs communication. A miscommunicated poach creates gaps and frustration.

followUps.line: Yeah, that one's on me. Next time I'll give you a signal before I go for the middle.
followUps.why: Shows you understand that communication makes poaching work.

followUps.line: I like the idea of a surprise poach, but only if we agree on a signal first.
followUps.why: Reframes poaching as a team tactic that needs trust.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Jordan is upset about losing the point. A warm apology and an offer to agree on a signal is better than explaining poaching.

payload.prompt: One opponent struggles on the backhand. Is it fair game to hit there?

scene.alt: Doubles scenario: choosing which opponent to target.

choices.label: No, always hit the stronger player

explanation.correct: Yes. Hitting to an opponent's weaker shot is a normal part of the game, like any other tactic, and it is how teams create errors.
explanation.incorrect: There is no rule or etiquette against it. Sending the ball to the weaker shot is ordinary strategy. Being kind about it afterwards is the polite part.
explanation.sayThisLine: Hitting to the weaker side is just part of the game.

payload.prompt: What is the main goal of targeting the weak side in doubles?

options.text: To force the weaker player to hit their worse shot, creating an error or weak return
To be mean to the weaker player
To tire them out
To confuse the stronger player

explanation.correct: Sending the ball to a player's weaker shot makes errors and weak returns more likely, which is how teams win points.
explanation.incorrect: It is not about being mean or about tiring anyone out. It is ordinary strategy: make the other team play their weaker shot.
explanation.sayThisLine: I aim for the weaker shot to create errors.
